            Singing together. In a community choir, 90 minutes of singing raised closeness, positive mood and pain thresholds, a stand-in for the release of endorphins, by a similar amount in small groups and in a choir of 232 (Weinstein et al., 2016). In new adult education classes followed for seven months, singers felt close to each other sooner than people in craft or creative-writing classes, who caught up later: the ice-breaker effect (Pearce et al., 2015). Moving in time together and endorphins may both be at work, in music as in laughter, dance and sport done together (Tarr et al., 2014). Sing Together uses two traditional rounds, so everyone sings at once and each group still has a part of its own; on your own, the phone takes the other part. No study has tested singing along with a phone.

            Nature sounds

            Natural sounds such as birdsong, wind and water are often, though not always, heard as pleasant and restful: songbirds more than the calls of gulls or crows, some animal sounds not at all, and people differ in which ones they like (Ratcliffe, 2021). In an experiment with 95 students, listening to birdsong raised heart-rate variability, a sign of less physiological stress, compared with traffic noise (Ford et al., 2026). The guide behind Entrain's new techniques rates nature soundscapes such as birdsong and rain as moderate evidence, and advises letting people choose, since some find certain sounds unpleasant. So the background sound is a mix you make: rain or crickets, with birdsong, a stream, wind in the leaves or a crackling fire added on top, each on or off by itself, under any practice, breathing session or track. You'll find it in Settings, on Breathe and under a practice's Options.

            A fire is the one sound with a study of its own. In three experiments with 226 adults, watching a fire with its crackle lowered blood pressure, and more the longer people watched, while the same fire with the sound off had no consistent effect (Lynn, 2014). That fire was seen as well as heard, so the crackle on its own hasn't been tested: here it's one more background sound, suited to the evening.

            Each is synthesised on your device, with no recordings. The birds are whistles that glide, warble and trill in the patterns of a robin, a blackbird, a great tit, a chiffchaff and a wren, with a wood pigeon cooing further off; the stream is noise in two bands with thousands of small bubbles whose pitch rises as they ring; the wind brightens and swells in gusts, with the rustle of leaves rising with it; and the fire is a low roar, a soft hiss and crackles in clusters, with pops and sparks on a loop of another length. The loops differ in length, so together they don't repeat for a long time.

            Sound and sleep

            Sound can deepen sleep, but only when it's timed. Short bursts of pink noise played in step with the slow waves of deep sleep, which an EEG watches for all night, raised slow-wave activity and next-morning word recall in older adults (Papalambros et al., 2017), and in 14 volunteers, bursts timed the same way also strengthened the flow of the fluid that clears waste from the brain (Levitt et al., 2026). The memory effect is less sure than the early studies suggested: across 14 studies with 206 participants it shrank year by year, and the memory test used was barely reliable from one night to the next (Harlow et al., 2023). Why Entrain can't do the timing is under what it leaves out.

            Noise played all night is a different thing. In a study of 72 students, those who slept with pink noise playing all night did no better at spotting a hidden rule in a puzzle than those who stayed awake, while those who slept in silence did a little better; the noise shortened the lightest stage of sleep, which went with insight. The authors suggest that overnight pink noise may cost some of what sleep does for insight and pattern detection, though few people found the rule, so it's far from settled (Vickrey & Lerner, 2023). The guide's advice is to avoid all-night noise as a default, and to offer timed or fading sound instead.

            That's what Sleep sounds does: pink noise, rain, crickets, a stream or a fire that fades out over 15, 30, 45 or 60 minutes and then ends by itself, even with the player set to open-ended. A fade like this hasn't been tested on its own; it keeps the sound to the time it takes to fall asleep. And when a track is left open-ended late at night with noise or a background sound under it, the player says so.

            Music: stress, tempo and taste

            Music lowers stress reliably, if modestly. In two meta-analyses of 104 randomised trials with 9,617 people, music interventions, mostly listening, had a small-to-medium effect on the body's signs of stress (d = 0.38) and a medium one on how stressed people felt (d = 0.55). Of the body's signs, heart rate came down most clearly, ahead of blood pressure and stress hormones (d = 0.46 against about 0.35; de Witte et al., 2020). With a trained music therapist the effect was medium to large, across 47 studies with 2,747 people (d = 0.72; de Witte et al., 2022). The guide behind Entrain's new techniques rates music for stress relief as strong evidence.

            Tempo moves brain waves in a predictable direction. In 26 adults listening to unfamiliar instrumental music at 56, 106 and 156 beats a minute, slow music raised theta and alpha power at the front of the head, a pattern that goes with relaxation, and fast music raised beta and gamma, with frontal alpha falling as the tempo rose (Yang et al., 2025). The guide rates slow-tempo music for relaxation as moderate to strong evidence, and fast-tempo music for energy and focus as moderate.

            Taste matters as much as tempo. A review of EEG research found that music a listener likes raises brain-wave power across the bands, most in beta and alpha over the right front and side of the head, while disliked music, improvisations and white noise didn't do the same (Kučikienė & Praninskienė, 2018). The same piece can work differently for two people, which is why the guide rates music you choose yourself as the strongest of the three.

            Entrain's music is made on your device as it plays, with no words and no recordings: soft chords, a low note under them and sparse plucked notes on a five-note scale, each chord following the last by chance, so it's never quite the same twice. Its tempo follows what a session is for: slow, about 60 beats a minute, for sleep and calm; steady, 96, for focus; lively, 124, for energy, with a soft pulse on the beat. Choose it as background sound in Settings, on Breathe or in the player, keep a choice for one practice under its Options, or take a Music Break: ten to twenty minutes with your eyes closed, which shows your heart rate at the start and the end against your usual when a heart sensor is connected. Tracks keep your heart rate at the start and the end in your history too, so you can see what each one does for you. This music hasn't been tested itself, and music you like does more, so pick the tempo you enjoy, or leave it off. A note that falls near a beat's carrier tone moves an octave away, so the music leaves a binaural beat alone.

            Scenes to watch: nature, fractals, flowers and fire

            What you look at matters too. In an early study, alpha waves, a sign of wakeful relaxation, were higher while people looked at slides of trees and plants than of city streets, and higher on average for water too (Ulrich, 1981). A study in Taiwan found alpha rising with the more restorative natural scenes (Chang et al., 2008), and video works as well: in 24 students, three-minute nature videos raised alpha more than city or abstract videos, most over the centre of the head, and were rated the most relaxing, though a memory task afterwards came out the same (Grassini et al., 2022). The guide behind Entrain's new techniques rates nature scenes as moderate evidence. Attention Restoration Theory explains them by soft fascination: drifting clouds, leaves, water and fire hold your attention without effort, which may let tired focus recover; and a setting restores best when it suits you, which the theory calls compatibility (Kaplan, 1995). That's why you pick the scenes you find restful.

            Many natural forms are fractals: the same kind of detail repeats at finer and finer scales, as in clouds, coastlines, trees and the outline of hills. How rough they are is measured as a fractal dimension, from 1 for a smooth line to 2 for one that fills the page, and the outlines in natural scenery mostly lie between about 1.3 and 1.5. In an EEG study of landscape silhouettes with different dimensions, the one at 1.3 gave the highest frontal alpha (Hägerhäll et al., 2008), and Taylor's group reports that fractals of mid complexity lower physiological stress, by as much as 60% on its measures of skin conductance and EEG, from work its first paper called preliminary (Taylor, 2006). Its explanation, fractal fluency, is that our eyes grew up among natural fractals and take them in with little effort (Taylor & Spehar, 2016). The guide rates fractals as promising: the findings come mostly from one lab and haven't been widely repeated by others. Entrain's fractal is ridgelines made the way fractal landscapes are, from waves each about twice as fine and a little less tall than the last (a Weierstrass-Mandelbrot curve), with a dimension of 1.4 by construction, drifting slowly past one another. Counted in boxes on a phone-sized drawing, over the few scales a screen can show, it comes out a little lower, at about 1.25.

            Fresh flowers have a small research record of their own, mostly from Yoshifumi Miyazaki's group in Japan. Office workers who looked at a vase of thirty pink roses for four minutes showed more of the heart-rate variability that goes with rest, and felt more comfortable and relaxed, than with no flowers (Ikei et al., 2014). Pooled across 214 people in such studies, from high school students to older adults, the roses seemed to even things out: fight-or-flight activity fell in those who started high and rose in those who started low (Ikei et al., 2023). The guide rates this as early: one group, and real roses only. Flowers on a screen haven't been tested, so Entrain's flowers are simply something gentle to look at, and real flowers on your desk are what was studied.

            The fire comes from the study under nature sounds: watching a fire with its crackle lowered blood pressure, and more the longer people watched, while the same fire with no sound had no consistent effect (Lynn, 2014). That fire was on a screen, so a fire to watch is one of the scenes, and it always comes with its crackle, even with the background sound off. The guide rates it as moderate evidence, and best in the evening.

            Each scene is drawn on your device as it plays, with no video and nothing downloaded: drifting clouds, rippling water with glints of moonlight, leaves swaying on a branch, a misty forest ridge, the fractal ridgelines, flowers and the fire, all moving slowly. On Breathe, choose Scene under Visual and one part of it follows your breath: as you breathe in, the sun rises, the moon's path on the water grows, the branch lifts, the mist rises, the light behind the ridges grows, the flowers open and the flames rise. In a practice, a scene can take the place of the orb, under Options. Pick the ones you find restful in Settings. With reduced motion turned on in your device's settings, each scene stays still, and on Breathe only its light follows your breath. These drawings haven't been tested themselves.

            Nature breaks: rest for tired attention

            Attention Restoration Theory, from Rachel and Stephen Kaplan (Kaplan & Kaplan, 1989), divides attention in two. Directed attention is the effortful focus of work and study, which holds distractions at bay and tires with use. Involuntary attention is drawn without effort by things that are gently interesting, which the theory calls soft fascination: clouds drifting, leaves moving, birds, running water, a fire. Resting directed attention while soft fascination holds you is meant to let it recover. A setting restores best when it takes you away from your usual demands, has enough in it to take in, holds your interest easily, and suits what you want to do: someone who hates hiking won't be restored by a forced trail walk (Kaplan, 1995). Stress Recovery Theory adds that nature calms the body directly, as a quick emotional response (Ulrich et al., 1991), and the two are usually seen as complementary.

            The study that tested it most directly had 38 students do a draining memory task, then walk for about 50 minutes, through an arboretum or along a busy city street, taking the other walk a week later. After the walk among the trees they could repeat about one and a half more digits backwards than before; after the city walk, about half a digit more, which wasn't a reliable change. Their mood improved more among the trees too, but that didn't explain the gain. In a second experiment, 12 people looked at photographs for about ten minutes, and only nature, not city streets, improved the effortful part of an attention test (Berman et al., 2008).

            How well it holds up: across 31 studies, a systematic review found that nature helped on three measures, repeating digits forwards and backwards and a test of switching between tasks, while the other ten of its pooled analyses showed no marked benefit, from small studies that measured attention in different ways (Ohly et al., 2016). A second review found working memory and cognitive flexibility improved, attentional control less reliably, and that studies meant different things by directed attention and tested it in different ways (Stevenson et al., 2018). Critics call ideas such as soft fascination vague, and say the claim that nature truly restores something used up hasn't been properly tested (Joye & Dewitte, 2018). The guide rates restoration breaks as moderate evidence: nature does seem to help some kinds of attention, especially working memory and switching between tasks, but which, and why, remain open questions.

            In Entrain, a Restoration Break puts this into a few minutes between blocks of work: one of the scenes you find restful, the theory's compatibility, with the nature sound that suits it, one line to begin, then no voice, captions or tasks, since anything that takes effort to read works against soft fascination; the guide calls that plausible, following the theory, rather than tested. It's offered at the end of the Focus Primer, when the Deep Work Block ends, and when you end the custom primer's working phase. Its end points you outside, as the guide suggests, to real nature rather than only a screen: Walking Meditation has a version for a park, whose guidance turns to clouds, leaves, birds and water. Fireside is the fire from the scenes, with its crackle, for 20 to 45 minutes in the evening: the relaxation grew the longer people watched, though in the study no one watched for more than 15 minutes (Lynn, 2014). And on your desk, real flowers, which are what the rose studies used (Ikei et al., 2014): a tip in the day's routine.

            Light colour: bright, warm and red

            Light reaches the brain by a second route besides sight. Cells in the eye that contain melanopsin, most sensitive to blue light at around 480 nm, feed the body clock and the systems that keep you alert. Brighter light makes people more alert and quicker, lowers the EEG activity in the theta and low alpha range (5–9 Hz) that goes with drowsiness, and holds back the sleep hormone melatonin at night (Sletten et al., 2021). Blue LED light in the evening lowered alpha power, in keeping with more alertness, in a small study of nine young men (Kayaba et al., 2014). Cool white light at 6500 K held back melatonin more than warmer light did, and gave faster reactions in tasks that need sustained attention (Chellappa et al., 2011), and a 2025 preprint, not yet peer reviewed, also found blue or blue-enriched light more alerting than warmer light of longer wavelengths. The guide behind Entrain's new techniques rates this as strong evidence, from body-clock research, and calls it the safest of the light techniques.

            The effect depends on the time and on the person. In morning types, blue light in the afternoon brought more of the slower theta and low alpha waves than white light did, which may mean they were less alert then: a preliminary finding (Siemiginowska & Iskra-Golec, 2020). In one small study of 24 men, evening types showed more of the fast beta waves that go with alertness under green light than people in between did, and its authors concluded that green light alerts evening types best (Vani et al., 2025). The results are mixed, too: in adolescents and young adults, blue light of two strengths, against a dim orange light, left alpha and theta power unchanged (Sharifpour et al., 2025). And light in the evening costs sleep: after two hours of blue-enriched light at 6500 K in the evening, deep slow-wave activity was lower in the first cycle of sleep (Chellappa et al., 2013).

            Entrain follows the guide's table with a screen light, in Settings, on Breathe and under a practice's Options. Bright is cool and near-white, for focus and energy in the morning; Warm is amber and dimmer, with less blue, for winding down in the evening; Night is very dim and red, with no blue at all, for the time before sleep. Warm and Night lay a colour over the whole screen, so every part of it, a scene too, keeps only the warm part of its light, and for Night only the red. Automatic picks one from what the session is for and the time of day: Bright for focus and energy by day and Warm from the evening on; the usual screen for calm, recovery and reflection by day, Warm in the evening and Night late at night; for sleep, Warm in the day and Night from the evening on; and Night on any practice's sleep steps. You can say whether you're a morning person, an evening person or in between: a morning person's times come an hour earlier, and Automatic leaves Bright out of their afternoon, as the study of morning types suggests; an evening person's come an hour later, with Bright in green if they like, from that one small study. Today's suggestion follows the same times.

            A phone screen gives far less light than daylight or a light box. Light and sleep researchers recommend at least 250 lux at the eye by day, counting the light the body clock responds to, and no more than 10 in the three hours before bed (Brown et al., 2022). A light box gives 10,000 lux at your eyes, and daylight outdoors gives thousands even on a cloudy day, while a screen at reading distance gives a small fraction of either. So for alertness, daylight comes first, as in the morning routine, with a light box on dark winter mornings; a screen's own light matters most in the evening, when less is better. Bright, Warm and Night haven't been tested on a phone screen: they follow the research on light at the eye, at a far smaller dose. A web page can't set your phone's brightness, so turn it up for Bright and down for Night.

            Touch: slow strokes, a hand on the heart, weighted blankets and massage

            Slow, gentle stroking. Hairy skin, like the forearm's, has nerves of its own for caress-like touch: C-tactile fibres. Stroked with a soft brush, they fired most at 1 to 10 cm a second, the speeds people rated the most pleasant (Löken et al., 2009), and they carry touch to the insula, a part of the brain that deals with feelings from the body (Olausson et al., 2002). Stroking the forearm at 3 cm a second was rated more pleasant than at 30 cm a second and slowed the heart more, and only on the forearm did it stir the muscles of a smile (Pawling et al., 2017). In 9-month-old babies, stroking at 3 cm a second slowed the heart, while slower and faster stroking didn't (Fairhurst et al., 2014). A review sets this touch among the ways close contact calms the body's stress responses (Kidd et al., 2023), and it may work partly through oxytocin, a hormone of bonding, though that link is still a proposal (Walker et al., 2017). Soothing Touch paces your own strokes at about 3 cm a second, one on each long breath out. Its speed on the screen comes from the screen's size, which you can match to a bank card, since a phone shows a CSS centimetre at about six tenths of a real one. A soft brush or a piece of velvet is an optional extra; the guide rates the evidence for soft textures as early.

            A hand on your heart, or a hug. In a randomised trial with 159 adults, 20 seconds of self-soothing touch just before a stressful mock job interview, most often a hand on the chest and the other on the belly with a few deep breaths, and a 20-second hug from someone else both lowered the rise of the stress hormone cortisol, compared with making a paper plane; heart rate and how stressed people felt stayed the same (Dreisoerner et al., 2021). Most of the participants were young women studying psychology, and the trial couldn't rule out other explanations, such as positive feelings or extra attention. The guide rates a hand on the heart or a self-hug as early to moderate evidence: a simple, calming add-on. Soothing Touch offers both.

            Weighted blankets. In a Swedish randomised trial of 120 outpatients with depression, bipolar disorder, generalised anxiety disorder or ADHD and insomnia, four weeks under a chain blanket of 6 to 8 kg eased insomnia far more than a light one did, a large effect (Cohen's d = 1.90), with no serious side effects (Ekholm et al., 2020). In a pilot trial of 102 adults with insomnia, a 5.5 kg blanket improved sleep quality after a month, with less daytime sleepiness, stress and anxiety (Yu et al., 2024). Across five trials in people with mental disorders, anxiety fell a little, a standardised mean difference of 0.40 (Zhao et al., 2024). So a weighted blanket is a low-risk option with moderate support for adults whose restlessness at night has an anxious or low edge, and unproven for most other people. Choose one you can easily push off by yourself: it's not for small children, or for anyone who couldn't take it off unaided. Sleep Descent and healthy sleep habits suggest one.

            Massage and alpha. A shift towards alpha waves is one of the most consistent findings in EEG studies of massage: across 30 of them, a single session commonly raised alpha and lowered faster beta and gamma activity, and moderate pressure favoured a relaxed, parasympathetic profile; in one, a moderate-pressure Swedish massage lowered the slow delta and theta waves and raised alpha at the front of the head (Chmiel & Kurpas, 2026). Not every study agrees. In 24 young adults, a massage by hand and one by a device changed delta, theta and beta differently, and alpha fell during that short session in both (Chang et al., 2012). Almost all of this research is on massage from a trained therapist; massage you give yourself, or a partner, has been studied far less. Self-Massage walks you round the hands and forearms, jaw and temples, scalp, neck and shoulders and feet with moderate pressure, or takes turns with a partner.

            Temperature: cold and heat

            Cold water. Cold gives a fast, strong boost to the body's alertness chemicals, and to mood. In 10 healthy men, an hour sitting in water at 14 °C raised noradrenaline by about 530% and dopamine by about 250% (Šrámek et al., 2000). In 33 adults new to cold water, five minutes up to the collarbones at about 20 °C left them feeling more active, alert, attentive, proud and inspired, and less distressed and nervous, and in a brain scan afterwards large brain networks were more strongly connected (Yankouskaya et al., 2023). After 15 minutes at 10.5 °C, cortisol hadn't changed half an hour later but was 47% lower three hours later, in a small study of eight adults (Reed et al., 2023). The guide rates cold exposure as moderate evidence for alertness and a better mood, with a real safety risk. All of these were baths, colder or longer than the end of a shower: a cold finish to a shower is the gentle start the guide suggests, 30 to 60 seconds of it for morning energy, and it hasn't itself been measured this way. Cold Finish times 15 seconds to a minute of it, building up over the weeks, with loud cues to breathe out long and slow through the gasp, and a bell to turn the water cold and another to turn it off; the morning routine and the end of Morning Wake-Up suggest it. Cold water, in Healthy living, covers cold plunges too.

            Cold shock. Sudden cold water sets off a gasp, fast breathing and a jump in heart rate and blood pressure: the cold shock response, the main danger of cold water and a common start to drowning (Tipton et al., 2017). It is riskiest with a heart condition or high blood pressure. So start gradually, with the end of a shower; never go into cold open water alone; and never combine cold water with Wim Hof breathing or breath holds. The health check adds a caution written for you, and Cold Finish asks for it first.

            Heat. In a randomised trial, 34 adults with major depression had a single session of whole-body heating in an infrared chamber, until their core temperature reached 38.5 °C (about an hour and three quarters), then an hour's rest as they cooled, or a convincing sham. Depression eased more after the heating, and the difference lasted the six weeks of follow-up (Janssen et al., 2016). It used a specialised medical machine, not a sauna, and direct evidence that regular saunas ease depression or anxiety is still limited: a review of 40 studies of regular dry saunas found mostly benefits, but few good trials, with better mood and less anxiety in small, mostly uncontrolled studies, and links in large population studies that may not be cause and effect (Hussain & Cohen, 2018). The guide rates heat as early to moderate evidence for relaxation and mood. A warm bath in the evening is better supported for sleep: across 13 studies, about 10 minutes at 40 to 42.5 °C, one to two hours before bed, helped people fall asleep about 10 minutes sooner (Haghayegh et al., 2019). Sauna and heat and the evening routine pair it with a relaxation or sleep practice. Drink water, skip saunas after alcohol, and with a heart condition, low blood pressure or pregnancy, ask a doctor first.

            Air, scent and chewing gum

            What you breathe matters as well as how you breathe. In a controlled study at Harvard, 24 office workers spent six full working days in the same office, without being told what changed from day to day. On the day its air held few of the chemicals given off by paint, cleaning products and furniture (volatile organic compounds), their scores on a test of decision-making were 61% higher than on the day with a typical office's air, and on the two days with more fresh air on top, 101% higher. Carbon dioxide (CO₂) and those chemicals each went with lower scores on their own (Allen et al., 2016). As a later study sums that one up, ventilation of 20 cubic feet a minute per person, with CO₂ above about 900 ppm, went with significantly lower scores; the later study itself, following 302 office workers in six countries for a year, found their answers on short tests a little slower and less accurate as CO₂ rose (Cedeño Laurent et al., 2021). At home the levels are usually lower: in 206 people working from home for a year, most readings were under 640 ppm, and a slight link between more CO₂ and poorer scores on one test remained, short of statistical significance (Young et al., 2024). The guide rates fresh air for clear thinking as strong evidence.

            So the page of each focus practice and focus track, and the custom primer, can remind you to air the room first (Air the room before focus sessions, in Settings), and shows your room's CO₂ when there's a reading from the last two hours: from an Aranet4 monitor connected over Bluetooth, or a number you type in from any monitor, on the Heart page's Room air. Above about 900 ppm it says to open a window. Outdoor air holds about 420 ppm, so a few minutes with a window open brings the room's air down towards it. The same reminder is a step in the day's routine.

            Scent. In a classic study, 40 adults breathed lavender or rosemary for three minutes and did simple sums before and after. With lavender, beta power in the EEG rose, which the authors read as drowsiness; people felt more relaxed and less depressed, and did the sums faster and more accurately. With rosemary, frontal alpha and beta power fell, which they read as alertness, and people felt more alert (Diego et al., 1998). It's a small, older study, and the authors' reading of lavender's EEG is unusual, since more beta normally goes with alertness. The guide rates rosemary for alertness as early evidence and lavender for relaxation as early to moderate, so Entrain offers each as an optional tip, never a need: rosemary on focus pages, and lavender on sleep pages and in an evening routine, each with the scents line from the safety notes, since some people react to essential oils and some oils are harmful to pets. The tips can be turned off in Settings.

            Chewing gum. The best-studied effect in taste comes from chewing gum rather than flavour, and it's a mild one. In experiments, people felt more alert while chewing gum, and in a study of a working day, chewing went with getting more done and fewer cognitive problems; it raised cortisol in the morning and left the heart rate alone, though chewing has raised the heart rate a little in laboratory studies. Under stress the findings are mixed: some studies found cortisol fell with gum, others that it rose (Allen & Smith, 2015). A 2025 review of 32 brain-imaging studies found that chewing, flavoured gum most of all, briefly heightened alertness, which faded soon after the chewing stopped, and its authors caution that the changes in the brain can't yet be tied directly to the benefits (Chmiel & Malinowska, 2025). A 2022 meta-analysis reporting that chewing gum eases anxiety and stress was retracted by its publisher in 2023 and shouldn't be relied on (Luo et al., 2022). The guide rates gum for alertness as early to moderate evidence, so Entrain offers it as an optional tip on focus pages, before work.

            The mind: guided imagery and yoga nidra

            Hypnosis and guided imagery. An overview of 49 meta-analyses of hypnosis from the last 20 years, covering 261 studies, found medium to large effects on distress, anxiety included, in people undergoing medical procedures, and only very small or small effects on physiological measures; just nine of the meta-analyses were of high quality (Rosendahl et al., 2024). In the US Department of Veterans Affairs' map of the evidence, guided imagery significantly reduced anxiety or tension in 4 of 6 studies of people having heart surgery, though the reviewers' confidence was low; across the other groups studied, the findings were mixed, with low confidence overall (Freeman et al., 2019). In the EEG, hypnosis has been linked most closely with more theta and with changes in gamma activity (Jensen et al., 2015), and it often uses imagery and slow, deep breathing to deepen relaxation. The guide rates hypnosis and guided imagery as moderate to strong evidence for less anxiety, and easy to pair with breathing. Most of the research is on hypnosis given by a clinician, or on recordings in hospital; imagery you do on your own at home has been studied less. Guided Imagery follows the usual pattern of a hypnotic relaxation: longer breaths out with your eyes on one spot, the eyes closing, a count down from ten to one, a calm place you choose explored through each sense, a suggestion you choose, and a count back up from one to five, or on into sleep.

            Yoga nidra. Yoga nidra, “yogic sleep”, sometimes called non-sleep deep rest (NSDR), is guided rest lying down that keeps you between waking and sleep, in the drowsy, inward state where theta rises. In the form Swami Satyananda Saraswati taught, it moves through set stages: a resolve, the sankalpa; a quick rotation of awareness round the body; the breath, counted backwards; pairs of opposite feelings such as heavy and light, warm and cool; quick images; and the resolve again (Satyananda Saraswati, 1976). In a small brain-imaging study, the release of dopamine in the striatum rose during yoga nidra, along with more theta in the EEG (Kjaer et al., 2002). In a randomised trial of 41 adults with chronic insomnia, yoga nidra and cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia both improved sleep time and sleep quality; in the sleep lab only yoga nidra added deep sleep, and its salivary cortisol fell (Datta et al., 2021). An online yoga nidra based on a body scan reduced stress slightly over two months, and its 30-minute version reduced sleep disturbance (Moszeik et al., 2025). The guide rates yoga nidra as moderate evidence for deep relaxation, a fit for deep rest and for sleep. Its stages haven't been tested one by one. Yoga Nidra takes you through them in 20, 30 or 45 minutes, each point of the rotation lit and marked on the body map, and ends back to alert or, at bedtime, on into sleep.

            With care. Both can play a 6 Hz theta beat underneath if you add it, sliding down to 3 Hz delta as you drift into sleep; the beats' own evidence is mixed, as the evidence explains. Expectation plays its part in any relaxation, and deep relaxation can bring up memories or strong feelings, or leave you feeling detached or unreal (placebo and side effects). With psychosis or a dissociative disorder, now or in the past, talk to your doctor or therapist first; the health check adds a caution written for you. You can open your eyes at any moment, and I need to stop ends a session in one tap.

            Expectation, placebo and side effects

            Recent breathwork trials compare a real technique with a convincing fake that people expect just as much from. In 400 adults, about ten minutes a day of coherent breathing at about 5.5 breaths a minute for four weeks improved stress, anxiety, depression and wellbeing, but no more than a placebo pace of 12 breaths a minute that participants found just as credible (Fincham et al., 2023). In the largest blinded trial of its kind, 200 adults did 20 minutes a day of fast breathing with breath holds, in the style of Wim Hof, or a placebo version, for three weeks; both groups expected the same, and stress improved in both by the same amount (Fincham et al., 2024). So much of breathwork's benefit seems to come from the practice itself (daily time out, relaxing the body, attention on the breath, and expectation) rather than from the exact pattern. Both trials were in healthy adults rather than patients, and in a month-long trial cyclic sighing still lifted mood more than mindfulness meditation (Balban et al., 2023).

            Expectations shape results. In the Wim Hof immune study, men who expected more of the training reported fewer flu-like symptoms, and the more optimistic had more adrenaline and more of the anti-inflammatory signal IL-10 (van Middendorp et al., 2016). Expectancy, arguably the main part of the placebo effect, changes the effects of many treatments, mind-body practices among them. That's why each technique here states its evidence as it stands, and why the end screen sets your own numbers against your usual: honest expectations, and a way to see what works for you.

            Side effects. Meditation can have them. Across 83 studies with 6,703 participants, 8.3% had an adverse event: 3.7% in experimental studies and 33.2% in observational ones. The most common were anxiety, depression and cognitive anomalies, and they could happen to people with no history of mental health problems (Farias et al., 2020). If a practice brings up strong feelings, open your eyes, look around the room and breathe slowly, and talk to someone you trust or a professional if it keeps happening; the safety notes say who should check with a clinician first.

            How often and how long

            Spreading practice across the day seems to work better than long single blocks, and how often you practise predicts benefit better than how long each session lasts. No study was found that compares back-to-back sessions with spaced ones directly.

            • Resonance breathing. The original protocol for heart-rate-variability biofeedback prescribed 20 minutes twice a day, with a warning to breathe naturally rather than overbreathe (Lehrer et al., 2000). Across studies since, people usually practise for 5 to 20 minutes once or twice a day at their own resonance rate (Lalanza et al., 2023). One practice guide suggests keeping home practice to 20 minutes a day, for a risk that is only theoretical; that is a minority, precautionary view.
            • Meditation. In a 2025 study that followed meditators over time, how often they practised predicted wellbeing, mood and distress better than how long they sat, and change worth noticing came with more daily practice than is usually advised: about 35 to 65 minutes a day for wellbeing and 50 to 80 for mental health (Bowles & Van Dam, 2025). The standard eight-week mindfulness courses ask for about 45 minutes of practice at home six days a week, and people do about two thirds of it on average (Parsons et al., 2017). In about 280,000 sessions in a meditation app, session length made no overall difference, while practising consistently, four to seven days a week, went with the largest improvement (Cearns & Clark, 2023).
            • In practice. Gentle practices (slow breathing, meditation, a body scan) can add up to longer daily totals when they're spread over separate sessions, such as a morning, a midday and an evening one. Intense techniques, such as Wim Hof-style breathing, belong in short sessions rather than long back-to-back blocks, because of the risk of fainting.

            Combining techniques. Studies rarely test whether effects add up when techniques are stacked. In a pilot trial with 60 healthy adults, resonance breathing guided by live music raised well-being and heart-rate variability more than listening to recorded relaxation music (Fuchs et al., 2018). Entrain's programmes put together techniques whose evidence points the same way, as Guided practices explains, but the combinations themselves haven't been tested, so your own numbers after each session are the best guide.

            What to measure

            Heart rate, heart-rate variability and breathing rate can all be measured well at rest, which suits breathing and meditation. How you feel may be the most important measure of all: a quick rating before and after.

            Signals worth measuring, what they show, and whether Entrain reads them.
            SignalWhat it showsIn Entrain
            Heart rateArousal and calming. Good at rest from a chest strap, a watch or ring, or a fingertip on a phone's cameraHeart, with a Bluetooth sensor or the phone's camera
            Heart-rate variabilityThe balance of calm and stress, and breathing coherence. A chest strap is the most accurateHeart, with a sensor that sends the time between beats, or the phone's camera
            Breathing rateWhether you're actually following the guided paceBreath from the microphone, or the phone on your belly on Breathe
            Finger temperatureRelaxation: the hands warm as their blood vessels widen, and stress cools the fingertips most (Vinkers et al., 2013)A web page can't read it
            Skin conductanceMoment-to-moment stress and arousal. Sensitive, but consumer devices are less reliable: a Fitbit Charge 5 agreed only moderately at best with a research device (Ko et al., 2025)A web page can't read it
            Blood oxygenA rough safety signal during breath holds. A wrist reading is less accurate than a fingertip oximeterBlood oxygen on Heart, from a fingertip oximeter: a hold ends below 90%
            Movement, stillnessSettling down, restlessness, sleepStillness, on the end screen of practices done lying down
            EEGBroad brain-wave trends only, as measuring at home explainsBrain trends on Heart, from a Muse headband
            How you feelWhat you actually feel, the main measure in most stress researchStress Check, which asks first

            Most of the validations were done at rest, which suits breathing and meditation. Stress shows best in several signals together, such as the heart, skin conductance and breathing: in one validation, combining them detected laboratory stress a little more accurately than any one alone (Darwish et al., 2025). And as with EEG, changes over a session and over weeks say more than a single “you are stressed” verdict, which is why the end screen sets each number against your own usual.

            Blood oxygen. A pulse oximeter shines red and infrared light through a fingertip and works out how much of the blood's haemoglobin carries oxygen, the SpO₂; at rest it usually reads 95 to 100%. A breath hold lowers it, and long holds after fast breathing can take it low before the urge to breathe comes, which is how people black out (see breath training for swimming and diving). A fingertip oximeter is more accurate than a watch at the wrist or a ring, but even its reading trails the blood by several seconds, so it's a rough safety signal, never a reason to hold on. On the Heart page, Entrain connects to a fingertip oximeter that uses Bluetooth's standard pulse oximeter service; while a breath hold runs, in Wim Hof Breathing or on Breathe, a reading below 90% ends the hold at once, with “Breathe now”. It only ever ends a hold sooner. That's Entrain's own rule, from general knowledge rather than a trial.

            Measuring with the phone alone

            A fingertip on the phone's camera, lit by its light, shows each heartbeat: as blood fills the fingertip it lets a little less light through, the principle of a pulse oximeter. Read this way, two apps measured heart rate far more accurately than two that read the face from a distance, against an ECG in 108 hospital patients (Coppetti et al., 2017), and a review of ten studies found that fingertip readings at rest agreed closely with an ECG, though only under tightly controlled conditions; few of them reported their participants' skin tone (Mather et al., 2024). The time between beats holds up too: RMSSD from a fingertip agreed almost perfectly with an ECG at rest (Plews et al., 2017), and during biofeedback at paces from 6.5 down to 4.5 breaths a minute, where the resonance pace it found matched the ECG's for about three people in four (van Dijk et al., 2023). Skin tone matters for any reading made with light: a large study of a phone's front camera reading the face during everyday use met the industry's accuracy standard across light, medium and dark skin (Liao et al., 2026). On the Heart page, Use the phone's camera reads your fingertip at rest and feeds each beat to the same numbers a chest strap does. Entrain's own way of reading it hasn't been tested against an ECG, or across skin tones, so it's marked experimental, and a signal meter shows when its beats are clean enough to count.

            Breathing rate can come from the phone's motion sensor. Laid on the chest, a phone's accelerometer agreed with airflow to within about 1.5 breaths a minute, in a preliminary study of five people (Estrada et al., 2015). On Breathe, Phone on your belly does this lying down: each breath tilts the phone a little, and the page finds the rhythm of that tilt over the last 45 seconds, then says beside the guide whether you're following it, faster or slower. It's Entrain's own reading, untested against airflow, and slow breathing needs a little longer to show.

            Stillness from the same sensor is the simplest of the three, and general knowledge rather than a tested measure: how much of a session the phone, resting on your belly or on the bed beside you, lay still, and your longest still stretch. Longer still stretches go with settling down, more movement with restlessness. A practice done lying down offers it under Options, and shows it on the end screen. All three are best read as trends over a session and over weeks, set against your own usual, rather than as verdicts.

            What Entrain leaves out, and why

            • Pink noise timed to deep sleep. Short bursts of sound timed to the slow waves of deep sleep raised slow-wave activity, and with it next-morning word recall, in older adults (Papalambros et al., 2017). It works only closed-loop: an EEG has to watch for each slow wave all night and play the sound at the right moment. A phone can't see your brain waves, and a web page can't keep that kind of timing all night with the screen locked, so this stays research for now.
            • Smart bulbs. A web page can't reach the bulbs in your home: they answer their makers' apps, or a hub on your home network that a secure web page isn't allowed to talk to. Set them yourself instead: bright and cool in the morning, dim and warm in the evening, very dim and warm or red before sleep. Entrain's screen light does the same for the screen.
            • EMDR. Eye movements while recalling a memory tax working memory, and in laboratory studies they made distressing memories less vivid and less upsetting (Jeffries & Davis, 2013). But EMDR is a therapy for trauma, given by trained clinicians, so Entrain has no self-guided version: trauma work belongs with a clinician.
            • Candle gazing and panoramic vision. No good-quality studies of trataka or panoramic vision were found, so Entrain makes no claims for them.
            • Skin temperature, skin conductance and health apps. Rings and watches keep skin temperature and skin conductance to their own apps, and Apple Health and Google Health Connect open only to apps installed on the phone, not to a web page. Entrain runs in your browser and sends nothing anywhere, so it reads what a page can: a Bluetooth heart sensor and the microphone.

            Safety

            Entrain is for everyday stress, sleep and focus. It isn't a medical device or a treatment: nothing here diagnoses, treats or prevents any condition, and its heart readings are for practice, not for checking your health. Talk to a clinician about problems with sleep, anxiety or attention.

            • The beats. Ask your doctor first if you have epilepsy or another seizure disorder: the beats are meant to nudge the brain's rhythms, and their safety for people with epilepsy hasn't been established. Never listen while driving, cycling on the road or operating machinery, since the slower beats are made to relax you or send you to sleep. Keep the volume low.
            • Headphones with a pacemaker. The magnets in headphones and earbuds can interfere with a pacemaker or an implanted defibrillator. Keep them at least 15 cm (6 in) from it: not around your neck or in a breast pocket (American Heart Association).
            • Breathing. Breathe gently, and stop to breathe normally if you feel light-headed, dizzy or tingly. Leave out the breath holds and the fast breathing (Wim Hof, Kapalabhati, Morning Wake-Up's breath of fire, the power breaths before sport) if you are pregnant or have a heart, lung or blood-pressure condition or epilepsy, and never do the fast breathing in or near water, in the bath, standing up or while driving. Rest for an hour between blocks of fast breathing or long holds: back to back, they make fainting more likely, so Restart and Do it again ask first, and Wim Hof stops at eight rounds a day.
            • Breath holds. Swim & dive's long holds are done entirely at your own risk. A breath hold can make you black out without warning, so practise them only on dry land, sitting or lying down, never in or near water, in the bath or while driving. Breathe normally before each hold, never fast and deep to stretch it, breathe whenever you need to, and keep the second inhale a gentle top-up rather than forcing in extra air. In the water, train breath holds only with a coach or a trained buddy watching you. A fingertip oximeter on the Heart page ends a hold that reads below 90%, but its reading trails the blood: it's a rough safety signal, never a reason to hold on.
            • Moving. Go only as far as is comfortable, stop anything that hurts, and keep clear space around you. Dancing and other brisk movement raise your heart rate: with a heart condition or high blood pressure, ask your doctor how hard to work, and rest if you feel dizzy, faint or very short of breath.
            • Feelings. A body scan, guided imagery, yoga nidra, tapping or a reflection can bring up strong feelings. If one does, stop, look around the room and breathe slowly, and talk to someone you trust or a professional if it keeps happening. While a practice or the breathing guide runs, I need to stop ends it in one tap, fades the sound and opens Settle: slow breaths out with your eyes open, and the 5-4-3-2-1 grounding.
            • Food and supplements. Supplements aren't checked like medicines, and some interact with them: ask a doctor or pharmacist before you start one if you take medicines (blood thinners above all), are pregnant or breastfeeding, have kidney or liver disease, or have an operation coming up. The amounts in Healthy living are those used in studies, not prescriptions.
            • Light. Ask a doctor before you use a light box if you have bipolar disorder or an eye condition, or take medicines that make you sensitive to light. Shield your eyes from red and near-infrared devices, and use a light box, never a tanning lamp, for light therapy.
            • Cold and heat. Cold water sets off a shock response, a gasp, fast breathing and a sudden rise in heart rate and blood pressure, which can be dangerous, above all with a heart condition or high blood pressure: ask your doctor first, and if you're pregnant too. Start gradually, with the end of a shower; never go into cold open water alone; and never combine cold water with Wim Hof breathing or breath holds. With a heart condition, low blood pressure or pregnancy, ask a doctor before saunas or very hot baths; drink water, and skip them after alcohol.
            • Scents. Some people react to essential oils, and some oils are harmful to pets. Use a drop or two in a diffuser or on a tissue, in an aired room; dilute an oil before it touches your skin, never swallow one, and keep them away from small children and pets, cats above all. With asthma, or in pregnancy, ask your doctor or midwife first, and stop if your chest tightens or your skin reacts.

            Check with a clinician before you start if you have a heart, lung or seizure condition, are pregnant, or are in treatment for anxiety, trauma or depression. Practices with cautions of their own give them in their introduction. The health check in Settings, optional and kept on your device, adds a caution written for you to the practices it affects; it never stops you starting one.

            Not medical advice. Binaural beats and paced breathing are self-help techniques, not treatments, and the effects reported in the literature are modest and vary from person to person. The safety notes say who should check with a doctor first.

            All audio is synthesised in your browser with the Web Audio API. Nothing is downloaded, streamed, recorded or sent anywhere.

            Quick headphone check

            A binaural beat only exists if each ear receives its own tone. On speakers, a single earbud, or a mono Bluetooth device the two tones mix before they reach you and nothing on this page does anything. This takes five seconds.

            A soft 440 Hz tone, sent to one ear only.

            Where did you hear it?

            Safety notes

            Swim & dive: read this first

              The research behind it is in Learn, under Breath training for swimming and diving.

              Rest first?

              Entrain's own rule, following the advice to cap rounds of intense breathing and leave out back-to-back blocks.

              Settle

              The session has ended and the sound is off. Keep your eyes open, and feel your feet on the floor and the seat under you.

              Then look around you: name five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell and one you can taste.

              If this keeps happening, or a practice often leaves you upset, talk to your doctor or a mental-health professional before you carry on with it. If you feel unsafe right now, call your local emergency number.

              Match a bank card

              Lay a bank card on the screen sideways, its top edge on the upper line; its far end can hang over the edge. Then size the box until the lower line meets the card's bottom edge.

              Top edge of the cardBottom edge

              Unlock the new techniques

              The techniques from the brain-wave guide open with a donation of €1 or more on Ko-fi, once on each device.

              1. Your device code:

              2. Donate €1 or more on Ko-fi and put this code in your message.

                Donate on Ko-fi

              3. You'll get an activation link by email. Open it on this device, or paste the code here.

              It unlocks this device and this browser only. On another device, or once this browser's data is cleared, a new donation unlocks it there. Backups don't carry it.

              Match your tinnitus pitch

              The notch has to sit on your tinnitus to do anything. Move the slider until the tone sounds closest to the pitch you hear, then save it. Keep the volume low — this is a pure tone.

              4000Hz

              Matches are commonly out by a whole octave, and which way depends on where you started from — so check the octave above and below before you settle.

              Above 8 kHz the notched-training trials found no significant effect. You can save this pitch, but expect the notch to do less than the trials reported.
              See a clinician first. Tinnitus that is new, one-sided, pulsing in time with your heartbeat, or paired with hearing loss or dizziness needs medical assessment. Sound therapy is an adjunct to care, not a substitute for it, and not a cure.
